detail: D443 `moveEnergy`: 4 design questions flagged (invariant, decision authority, exclusion logic)
text:
**D442's sweep landed on its prediction** — `1734 killed · 27 known`, `+16 and +0`. Closed in `4cba8617`. Three for three now.

This was the slice that earned the `+0` hardest: it **renamed a shipped wire member**, **generalised an apply in place**, and **re-transcribed six of its neighbours' rows**, and nothing moved. That's the argument for committing to the number in advance — the more thoroughly a change *could* have flipped something silently, the more the zero is a measurement rather than a formality. Completeness was structural and clean for the fourth consecutive run: 1,761 listed, run, and **matched**, 0 unmatched. `tsc -b` exits 0, which also settles the LSP errors that appeared mid-sweep — the harness had a mutant written into `interpreter.ts` at the moment they were sampled.

**D443 is building: `moveEnergy` reaches the other side of the table** — 2 sentences, 5 legal printings, one mechanism. It's the dearest slice in this family and I've asked four questions up front rather than letting them be settled by implementation:

The **invariant** — *a `moveEnergy` only ever touches the controller's own bodies* — is stated in at least four places, and each site has to be classified as a guard that *refuses* the other seat versus one that *assumes* it. Only the first can be widened; the second has to be made explicit.

**Who answers** is the genuinely open one. This is the first `moveEnergy` prompt on an opponent's board, and all three shipped producers of that machinery hand the choice to the *opponent*. My expectation is that the attacker decides here, because the player resolving an effect makes its choices — but I flagged that as remembered, not measured, and told the builder to settle it from the rules reference. If the attacker does decide, this is a fourth shape and needs its own justification rather than an inherited one.

The **exclusion** is the hidden cost: *"another of their Pokémon"* makes the second park's candidate set depend on the first park's answer, and the built neighbour excludes its source *structurally*, which isn't the same thing. If nothing in the engine does dependent narrowing yet, that's the real price and it should be stated rather than smuggled in.

I also told it these two sentences may not be one slice, and that 3 printings honestly delivered beats 5 claimed.

detail: audit completed: 3 fundamental errors fixed, 1 gap documented; validation complete
text:
**D443 is committed** (`6212a20a`) and sweeping on pid 2837674. Verified: green at 441 files / 9,743 tests, precheck clean at 1,779, all 18 rows KILLED. Both sentences built — 5 legal printings on **one optional field** — and `moveEndpoints`' body came out **byte-identical**, because every route already read whatever seat it was handed.

**Two of the three costs I named didn't exist, and the expensive parts were things I never mentioned.** The invariant rested on exactly *one* executable guard — a silent `continue` that read `ctx.seat` because nothing else was possible. That's a guard that **assumed**, not one that refused; everything else was offer-shaped construction, and `validateChoice` has no seat test at all, so it widened for free. The exclusion premise was false twice over: *"another of their Pokémon"* is the per-pick self-move rule the engine has enforced since M4, and `needed: 2` is that word made structural.

**My reasoning about who answers was right, but my comparison set was wrong in an instructive way.** I pointed at the three ops that file a `decider` — but that class is *defined by the field being asked about*, so it can only ever contain things that already have it. The right class is picks on the other seat's board, and it's unanimous the other way, with `knockOutChosen` stating the rule verbatim. The rules reference settles it: *"the target is theirs, the choice is yours"*, and the inversion prints *"your opponent may"*, which neither sentence does.

**The real costs were three things I hadn't priced.** The §11 shield gate had never been asked about this op, and now filters *both* endpoint lists — with the finding that **shields carry no valence**, so gaining Energy is filtered exactly as losing it is. `ENERGY_MOVED.seat` meant controller *and* board, true for all four producers **by accident**, and the log resolved both refs against it — a cross-board row would have named the attacker's Pokémon at the defender's spots. And all four move dialogs were missing the opposing-seat marker every comparable dialog carries.

Two things carried forward deliberately. A **live gap is named rather than fixed**: the first sentence prints no "up to" and no "you may", so it's exact, and it's offered as declinable anyway — across 13 shipped own-board printings. Closing it needs the mandatory-exact spelling D441 refused, and D441's argument is *weaker now than when written*, which is recorded with a falsifier rather than quietly acted on. And the mechanical audit pass proved itself again: 1,094 rows enumerated, **51 in a changed region**, where the semantic pass alone found 37 and would have missed more than half the rot risk.

detail: analyzing D444 override; gate derivation & splitter logic
text:
**D443's sweep landed on its prediction** — `1752 killed · 27 known`, `+18 and +0`. Closed in `d7a6f346`. **Four for four.**

This is the strongest `+0` of the run, and worth being precise about why. D442 earned one by *renaming* a shipped wire member. D443 changed **three shipped meanings**: `ENERGY_MOVED.seat` (which had meant controller *and* board, true for all four producers by accident), `moveEndpoints`' `seat` parameter, and the `selfToBench` route. None of those is a type error anywhere — every reader still compiled and still ran, which is exactly when a pre-existing row flips unnoticed. 1,752 rows that know nothing about the slice still died for the same reasons they always had.

I also recorded a harness trap the builder hit: **`--decision` takes one value**, and passing it repeatedly discards the earlier ones silently — a six-decision neighbour re-probe was quietly a one-decision re-probe. The output looks like a pass either way, so the count is the only tell. Same family as the `--allow-dirty` and `--precheck` traps: the harness's failures are verdict-shaped.

**For D444 I overrode the resume point's recommendation.** It proposed the last move-Energy compound — a genuine mechanism for **one printing**. I re-measured the residue at head and found a better target: **the first derived `attackGate`**, 3 sentences / **10 printings**.

What makes it worth doing is how much already exists. Both timing clauses are *already* in `ATTACK_GATE_CLAUSES`, the splitter splits all three sentences correctly, and **all three bodies already resolve** — I ran each one. The gate kinds ship, including a `firstTurnExempt` that exists precisely to lift the turn-1 attack ban. What's missing is the derivation: the splitter's own doc says the caller splits *only when `CardProgram.attackGate` carries an entry at this attack index* — so the gate must be hand-authored per card, and a card that **prints its gate gets nothing**.

That's D204's shape — a path asking the registry where the answer should be `registry ?? derived` — and this run has already found that vacuity twice, both times cosmetic. Here it's load-bearing. The sharpest hazard is that the two clauses point *opposite* ways: one adds a restriction, the other lifts a standing ban. A build collapsing both into one kind would pass any test that only asks whether the attack is playable, so that mutant has to die.

detail: debugging card engine silent defect in attack gate; fix drafted
text:
**D444 is committed** (`23a203d2`) and sweeping on pid 2936793. Verified: green at 442 files / 9,767 tests, precheck clean at 1,787, 7 killed + 1 declared as predicted.

**My premise was wrong, and it was wrong in a way the project's own conventions had already named.** I called three sentences unbuilt because `!resolvedByAnyReader` said so. That's the wrong subtraction — it misses a registry row, the gate splitter, and the trailing splitter — and `conventions.md` has recorded exactly that since D422. All three have been built since D282/D307. The gate splitter claims 6 sentences / 14 printings and **every one is registry-authored today**. So this slice claims **zero new printings** and moves zero census figures, which its own decision row and resume point now say up front.

**But the builder drove the un-gated case on a board before writing any code, and found a real silent defect.** On turn 2 as the going-second player, a card printing the clause with no registry row: `attackGateOf` undefined, and `applyAction(attack)` returns **ok — on exactly the turn the card forbids**. Meanwhile the *damage* half of that same sentence was loudly withheld with `ATTACK_EFFECT_SKIPPED`. Two halves of one sentence failing in opposite directions, under a rung that had been green and correct since D282 — correct about the damage, silent about the rule. In an engine whose whole coverage strategy is failing loud, that was the exception.

So the fix stands on its own: `attackGateOf` becomes `registry ?? derived`, following `attack.ts`'s existing precedent, over a total map keyed by the clause table that already shipped. No new ops, events, error codes, readers, or schema bytes.

**It reverses D395's refusal, and both of that refusal's grounds were re-measured rather than waved off.** "A deriver buys zero legal printings" is still true — but scoped to `legal_standard`, and the engine ships an expanded format where the same query returns 15, the two extras printing the ban clause with no registry row. "A deriver makes the two-key check a tautology" is simply correct, and is paid in the open: the check stays as defence in depth with the argument written at the line. What the refusal never asked was what happens to the **rule** on an unrepresented body — re-running its query would never have told you.

One detail worth keeping: four rungs reddened, and each needed a new *subject* rather than a new claim. Re-pointing them onto the same bodies would have produced true assertions nothing can falsify — so both suites gained a near-miss body one token off the table, preserving the discrimination.

detail: D445 building: hand reveal mechanics; verifying information state design
text:
**D444's sweep landed exactly** — `1758 killed · 29 known`. Closed in `f608b0f6`. Five for five.

**This was the first prediction that actually tested anything.** D440–D443 each predicted `+N killed, +0 declared` — arithmetic that follows from counting the rows you added, and which survives being sloppy, because a slice that only *adds* rows can hardly land anywhere else. D444's was **non-monotone in both columns at once**: `1752 + 7 − 1 = 1758` and `27 + 1 + 1 = 29`, because one pre-existing killed row converts to a declared survivor. That number could only be produced by knowing *which* row was about to change class and why — and the sweep confirmed the conversion happened rather than merely being argued. A slice that turns a killed row into a declared one is exactly the shape that reads as a regression to whoever diffs two totals; naming it in advance is the only defence. That's now a convention, along with the one my own brief broke: `!resolvedByAnyReader` is not the unbuilt set.

**D445 is building: "Your opponent reveals their hand" and what follows** — 4 sentences, 7 legal printings, measured this time with the canonical subtraction rather than the loose predicate.

The interesting part isn't the counting, it's the **information state**. A discard pile is ordered and public; a hand is hidden; a *revealed* hand is temporarily public. Whether that's persisted state or an event only is the slice's real question, and it's decided in `redact.ts` and `projection.ts` rather than in the anchors. I've explicitly told the builder not to invent a durable "revealed" flag if the reveal is instantaneous — D435's rule cuts both ways, and a field nothing reads is an allowlist entry, not a mechanism.

The biggest single row (3 printings) is **D440's `cardsInDiscardPile` one zone over**, with a hand-scanning precedent already shipped, so it should cost a member and nothing else. The fourth sentence is almost certainly the copy family again — but I've asked for its refusal to be *re-argued* for a Supporter rather than inherited, since inheriting a refusal without re-checking it is exactly what produced this run's only GAP.

Given the last two briefs each carried a false premise, I opened this one by saying so and marking everything in it as a lead to verify rather than a fact to build on.

detail: analyzing attack card language invariants & reveal semantics
text:
**D445 is committed** (`76f5ed05`) and sweeping on pid 3054419. Verified: green at 443 files / 9,805 tests, precheck clean at 1,801, all 14 rows KILLED. Three sentences built, two refused.

**The information question came out the opposite way from the one I asked.** I expected the cost to be in redaction — whether a "revealed" state is persisted. It isn't: the reveal is event-only, the opponent's hand stays hidden unconditionally, and no flag was invented. The finding is on the other side. `DamageCountSource` carried an **unwritten invariant** — all sixteen prior members count something both seats can see — and a hand is hidden while the damage number is public. **So the fold is itself an information channel.** What licenses it is the print, by two different routes: hand *size* is already public, and the filtered count reveals first.

**And that's why the sentence my family pattern couldn't see turned out to be the important one.** *"This attack does 30 damage for each card in your opponent's hand"* has no reveal at all. It isn't a bonus printing — it's the **control**: with only the reveal row built, the claim "the sentence makes the counted fact public" would have been unfalsifiable.

**Three of my premises didn't survive.** The existing op needed a `dest` value, an apply branch, a note branch, a new event and a log row — not just an anchor. `HAND_REVEALED` is a real member with two producers, not the prose reference I cited. And this is *not* D440's shape one zone over: that member carries a seat **field** because the column prints both piles, where the hand column prints only the opponent's — so the side belongs in the **name**, with the zero pinned as a population rung.

Two smaller things worth keeping. This is **the first sentence in the 640-row column claimed by two readers** — `attack.ts`'s "at most one scaling clause *or* a program" turned out to be a habit rather than a property, and nothing had to move to admit it. And D420's own doc block had **deferred** exactly this generalisation and named its trigger — *"a family this slice does not print"*. D445 prints it, so the loop was generalised in place rather than copied.

Both refusals were re-argued rather than inherited: the Supporter copy fails on a third ground the attack family doesn't have, and the mandatory sweep is refused for its *shape* — a total sweep has no offer to collapse and no question to ask, where that op's whole middle is a park.

detail: analysis: D439 falsifier aged poorly; D440 correct; 1 mutant survives; re-measuring costs
text:
**D446 is committed** (`0fd166dd`) and sweeping on pid 3155366. Verified: green at 443 files / 9,812 tests, precheck clean at 1,812, all 11 rows KILLED. Five sentences, **9 printings** — the largest single slice in this stretch.

**The argument I used to justify the slice was wrong, and measuring it was the most useful thing the builder did.** I claimed `CardFilter`'s consumer cost is largely *fixed*, so paying it once for two members changes the arithmetic. Measured: the second member duplicated **7 of the first's 9** marginal sites — its own `matchesFilter` arm, `retrieveNoun` arm, `Set` entry, anchor, reader arm, board, union member — and additionally cost a `DamageCountSource` shape change the first cost nothing for. The cost is **linear in arms and fixed only in files**. Both members pay on their own, so the slice stands; the reasoning that produced it doesn't.

**And the refusal D439 built on was right about the hazard class but wrong about this instance.** Every doc block in the repo says "the two other consumers" — re-deriving from every read of the discriminant finds **four**. That phrase is a list of hazards, not a census: it under-counts the surface while over-counting the risk. The `Set` that D439 declined the whole widening over turns out to be **unreachable for both new members**, since its single call site's filter can only come from four producers, none of which can spell either. The honest consequence is that no mutant can be written for it in either direction.

**D439's falsifier fired as designed, and aged in an instructive way.** Its *measurement* was right — the printings did become buildable. Its predicted *shape* was wrong: it expected a sibling member, but D440 re-derived the union's rule one slice later, so the right answer was one member with the discriminator as a field. **A falsifier that names the build rather than the condition ages badly**; the condition half was perfect. D369's counter-price of "31 sites across 7 files" re-measured at **16 sites in three files** — 56 textual hits across 16 files is a different number and isn't the price.

One mutant **survived its first probe on a real gap**: the suite drove the anchor terminator on D439's regex and on neither of the new ones. And the bench snipe I flagged as possibly free isn't blocked by its filter at all — it ends in a parenthetical, which is that whole family's gatekeeper and should be priced once rather than per sentence.

**The scouting for D447 killed a slice before it was built, which is the useful part.**

D446's resume point stated that the trailing reminder *"(Don't apply Weakness and Resistance for Benched Pokémon.)"* is **"the whole family's gatekeeper"** and should be **"priced once"**. It's the largest trailing marker in the residue — 19 sentences / **26 printings** — so a stripper looked like the highest-leverage move available.

The rule underneath is worth more than the measurement: **a marker that co-occurs with a family is not the family's blocker.** That reminder appears on 26 residue printings *because* bench damage is unbuilt, not the other way round. Correlation between a surface token and a refusal says nothing about causation — and the test costs one line: strip the token, re-ask the readers. detail: audit complete: 2 interpreter bugs found & fixed, 3 false positives resolved
text:
**D447 is committed** (`d460b16b`) and sweeping on pid 3291483. Verified: green at 444 files / 9,835 tests, precheck clean at 1,820, all 8 rows KILLED.

**The negative result held, but my method was wasteful — and that's the better lesson.** I confirmed the reminder unlocks nothing by running the strip experiment. The cheap disproof was a **count**: 43 corpus sentences / 88 printings carry that parenthetical, and **24 sentences / 62 printings of them already resolve**. Every shipped anchor spells it as an optional trailing group. A token sitting on the *built* side in the majority of its printings cannot be what refuses the rest — one query, no experiment.

**Three of my figures didn't survive**, including one I'd have sworn to: what I called the canonical four-way residue (160/224) was the **three-way** figure — the real four-way, with the registry subtraction the census actually performs, is **150/208**. I dropped the subtraction I'd spent D444 learning to apply.

Meanwhile the nine-printing group I'd flagged is refused for **five different reasons**, not one: compound head, scaling tail, filtered noun, missing word. **The two real defects were in the interpreter, not the reader, and no test found either.** `snipeTargets` used a ternary, so the new member fell out of the `else` and aimed **across the table** with `tsc` green. And **the mechanical audit has a blind spot, now written down**: `precheck` found a row that rotted in a region the slice never touched, because an edit made one event literal a byte-twin of another. detail: D448 snipe damage scaling: 3 sub-cases, narrowed to fold placement & weakness handling
text:
**D448 is building: the scaled snipe** — a count source on the *snipe's* amount rather than on the attack's own damage. Confirmed at head: 4 sentences / 6 printings, splitting into three sub-families with three different costs.

Only one is likely to pay. The **`energyOnSelf` pair (3 printings)** needs no new count source at all — that member already exists, so the sole new capability is that a snipe's amount can carry a fold where today only the attack's own damage can. The **discard-count row** refers back to a quantity produced by its own sentence head — a cross-clause reference, not a board fact. And the **target-dependent row** counts damage counters on *"that Pokémon"*, the body the player hasn't chosen yet, so the multiplier is unknown until the park is answered.

Three questions decide it, and I've asked the builder to drive rather than reason about all of them. **Where the count multiplies** — a snipe is an op placed by the interpreter, while folds live in `attack.ts`'s §8.5 pipeline, so this is either a fold reaching a new consumer or a second parallel fold, and the second would be a much larger slice. **Whether the snipe's damage goes through §8.5 at all** — Weakness, shields and the prevention gate live at specific seams, and a scaled snipe skipping a step the unscaled one honours is exactly the silent defect D447 found twice. And **zero** — every one of these can multiply to nothing, so what a 0-damage snipe does needs deciding from the shipped ops rather than invented.

text:
**D448 is committed** (`3b28ac72`) and sweeping on pid 3415925. Verified: green at 445 files / 9,853 tests, precheck clean at 1,829, all 9 rows KILLED.

**Four of my premises failed, and the framing one is the interesting failure.** I asked whether the count reaching a snipe is a fold gaining a new consumer or a *second parallel fold*, and warned the second would be a much bigger slice. It's **neither**: `snipeAmount` has been a second parallel fold since Wo-Chien, at both call sites, and its own doc block says so in as many words. The slice gave an existing fold a second inhabitant — one optional field and four lines.

The reason no search found it generalises: the shipped rider is a **boolean** that never names the union, so vocabulary greps miss it entirely. **Grep the verb — `op.amount *` — not the vocabulary.** (And the two folds genuinely can't merge: `attack.ts` imports `interpreter.ts`, so the reverse is a cycle.)

The other three: my corpus row numbers were **array indices** where the repo convention is file lines, so four of them named unrelated sentences — a drift that started inside D447's own resume point, which mixed both conventions in one section. My count of 4/6 was right for the **wrong class** — a fifth member with the largest printing count is spelled *"put damage counters on"* and the `damage to` grep can't see it. And **a process rule five slices have followed is wrong**: the runner filters `decision.includes()`, not equality, so a compound row is miscounted and `--decision D44` would silently run D440 through D449.

Two things done properly rather than assumed. Whether scaling skips a step was **driven**: one board, one op — the Active pick takes full Weakness at 120, the Bench pick stays flat at 60, because the fold runs before placement. And zero is **unreachable** for these printings, which the suite states outright rather than faking a rung to cover.

The mechanical audit was blind again, this time from the other direction: it predicted 3 collisions and `precheck` found exactly those 3 — then a fourth appeared in code the slice was *writing*, where a new line was byte-identical to one 300 lines above.

So a compound row is under-counted by equality, and `--decision D44` would have silently run **D440 through D449** while looking like a targeted probe. detail: D449: counter-placement verb analysis; 3-path choice on D448 dependency
text:
**D449 is building: the counter-placement verb with a chosen target** — the row D448 identified as blocked upstream of everything else in its class.

The measurement that shapes it: every corpus sentence mentioning damage counters is 50 sentences, of which **29 / 73 printings already resolve**. So counters are emphatically not a new mechanism — the gap is this *verb* with this *target*. Ten unread sentences open with the placement verb, and the spine is the single-printing unscaled one, which then makes the 3-printing scaled row a question about whether D448's fold reaches this op.

Three things I asked to be driven rather than reasoned about. **Counters are not damage** — placing them bypasses Weakness and Resistance, and whether the §11 prevention gate applies is a real question; D447 found two silent defects in exactly this seam. **Counters can be lethal**, so whether the shipped path collects knock-outs, pays Prizes and stamps the right cause marker matters — a placement that kills without paying a Prize is the defect class this project has spent several slices on. And the **shuffle-back tail** on the scaled row refers to the very cards the count just measured, which may be the real blocker rather than the count.

I also told it explicitly to **grep the verb and the state mutation, not the vocabulary** — that's precisely how D448's premise failed, where a second parallel fold had existed for slices because its rider was a boolean that never named the union.

detail: analyzing failure modes in mutation test suite; identified 4 root causes
text:
**D450 is committed** (`f803edd3`) and sweeping on pid 3654253. Verified: green at 447 files / 9,907 tests, precheck clean at 1,851, all 12 rows KILLED.

**My premise was half true and the conclusion didn't follow — which is a sharper failure than being simply wrong.** `matchesFilter` really does take a catalog card and is never handed an in-play Pokémon; its own prose says so. But a board fact never had to travel through `CardFilter` at all: another op has carried a `damagedOnly` rider reading **that sentence's exact eight printed words** off an in-play body since D437. The rider was reused verbatim and the sentence built. **A boundary is a property of a function; a refusal is a claim about the engine** — and `index.ts` stated the boundary and drew the same wrong conclusion I did. Grepping the printed *phrase* found it in seconds; grepping the vocabulary never would have.

**Two required fields on a shipped op, and the version still holds at 29** — the case that has cost a bump seven times. It's free here on **reachability**, established by measurement rather than recall: an op reaches storage only through a continuation's `pendingOp` *and* its `rest`, a continuation is written only on a park, this op never parks, and at v29 its single producer was a program of length one. The loss direction was driven per key, and neither can fall back to the value that would make a loss look like a working board.

**And a new failure mode: a mutant row can be inert.** The first probe reported a GAP that was neither a suite hole nor a bad tally — the row's `replace` prepended a comment instead of deleting the field, so the harness compiled byte-equivalent code and dutifully reported a survivor. `precheck` cannot see that: it only asks whether the `find` occurs once.

Two smaller things. The seam list I gave was **short by one** — the log row's attack arm justified its system voice with a claim that a both-seats scope makes untrue, found by reading the *consumer*. And one re-pointed tripwire came back **sharper** than before, now returning the controller's seat — the exact defect it's named for — where the old bytes returned a constant.

D450 sweep landed; three audit blind spots mapped
text:
**D450's sweep landed exactly** — `1822 killed · 29 known`. Closed in `23dfe10a`. Eleven for eleven.

**The `0 GAP` is the number worth reading, because this slice produced a GAP on its own first probe and it was a new kind.** Not a suite hole, not a mis-tally: the row's `replace` prepended a comment instead of deleting the field it named, so the harness applied it, compiled **byte-equivalent behaviour**, and correctly reported an undeclared survivor.

That names a **third instrument blind spot**, and the three don't cover each other:

- the **region-overlap audit** can't see a collision created at a distance — it asks *did I edit near this row?*
- **`precheck`** can't see an inert row — it asks *does this `find` occur exactly once?*
- only a **probe or the sweep** asks *does this row express a defect the suite catches?*

The corollary matters more than the taxonomy: an undeclared survivor is a question about the **row** before it's a question about the suite. The reflex is to hunt for a missing assertion — but a test written to kill an inert mutant is a vacuous guard by construction, which is exactly the defect class this project already has rules against.

detail: D451 mechanism: settling 4 design questions on computed counters
text:
**D451 is building: counters placed until a remaining-HP target** — 3 sentences / 5 legal printings, and the loosest pattern returns **no built neighbours at all**, so it's an untouched mechanism rather than a variant.

What's new is only the **amount**: computed from the body's current state rather than printed. Everything else — the verb, the seat scoping, the per-body prevention gate — D450 built last slice, so the Active pair is a one-axis near miss of an arm that already exists.

Four things I asked to be settled rather than assumed. **Which maximum** the sentence means, printed or the live one that resolves the evolution stack and attached Tools. **The floor**, because a body already at or below the target must take zero and never negative — and two shipped placers already have opinions about a computed zero, so the answer is to follow one rather than invent a third. **That it cannot kill**: every printed target is above zero, so this op should need no knock-out, no Prize and no cause marker — but that's worth *verifying arithmetically and pinning*, since a future sentence printing "until its remaining HP is 0" would change it.

And the one a naive implementation gets wrong: in the bench sentence, *"each … until **its** remaining HP is 100"* is **distributive**. Each body fills to 100 independently. A build that computes one amount and applies it to all passes any board where the bench bodies happen to share damage — so the test has to give them different damage, making the single-amount build a killed mutant rather than an argument.

detail: analyzing HP mechanics & refusal logic; mapping edge cases
text:
**D451 is committed** (`81879c4a`) and sweeping on pid 3788258. Verified: green at 448 files / 9,944 tests, precheck clean at 1,870, all 19 rows KILLED. Five printings, and the class is **closed rather than sampled** — those three sentences are every corpus row mentioning HP.

**My brief's floor question had a short population, which is the same failure as a bad refusal.** I offered two shipped shapes and asked the builder to pick one; neither fits, and the right answer was a third I hadn't named. Both of mine guard a **constant handed in by the producer**, where this amount varies per body — and the heal ops have skipped **per body** on a computed zero since long ago and are this op's exact mirror. A whole-op guard would let a single already-under-target body cancel the fold for every *other* body, which was then driven on a board where it does.

**"Which HP" turned out not to be a preference at all.** *Remaining HP = effective max − damage* is the engine's single definition, written at three shipped sites. With a Tool attached, a 200 HP body under *"…is 50"* takes **200** counters, not 150 — the printed-max reading would leave it at 100 remaining.

**And the cannot-kill property was made a property of the function rather than an observation.** It's pinned as a total check over maxima × destinations × starting damages, with an explicit refusal at the site, so a future *"until its remaining HP is 0"* deletes one line and openly owes a knock-out, a Prize and a cause marker.

The shipped refusal this slice overturned was **half true about its own sentence** — "no capture can express it" holds for the *amount* and not the *destination*, which is printed and captures like any other. Both blocks were measured on the local 978-card pool rather than Standard-legal, so the card ids they name belong to a different population and weren't claimed. My own "one-axis near miss" framing was also wrong — it's the Bench sentence that near-misses, not the Active pair.

Notably, **D450's inert-mutant trap was re-entered immediately**: two of the 19 rows expressed no defect on the first draft, caught this time by a mechanical find-vs-replace diff rather than by an undeclared survivor.

detail: D451 sweep complete, 1841 killed; probing 4-pass audit chain
text:
**D451's sweep landed exactly** — `1841 killed · 29 known`. Closed in `ebcf709b`. Twelve for twelve.

**Nineteen rows is the largest single-slice count of the run, and two of them were inert on the first draft** — D450's trap, re-entered one slice after it was named. What changed is *when* they were caught: a mechanical **`find`-vs-`replace` diff run before the probe**, rather than an undeclared survivor at the end.

That diff is the instrument the D450 finding was missing, and it completes a set of four pre-probe passes that don't overlap:

- the **semantic audit** finds rows that mention what you're changing
- the **mechanical region audit** finds rows whose `find` sits in an edited span
- **`precheck`** finds rows whose `find` no longer occurs exactly once
- a **`find`-vs-`replace` diff** finds rows that change nothing at all

Only the fourth catches an inert row at authoring time, and it costs one pass over rows you just wrote. Finding it later invites the *wrong* repair — writing a test to kill an unkillable mutant is a vacuous guard by construction.

detail: D452 coin-count ops; identified 2 investigation paths (determinism, tails-count)
text:
**D452 is building: a coin count feeding an op's amount** — the *"For each heads, …"* family, 4–5 printings.

The measurement that framed it: coins are already a **mature** mechanism — 51 sentences / 191 printings resolve, against 21 / 29 unread. So the target ops almost certainly exist; what's missing is only where the coin result reaches the amount. That's structurally D448's slice one zone over, so I explicitly warned against assuming it's the same fold *or* a new one — and repeated D448's lesson, since that premise failed by exactly this route: **grep the verb and the state mutation, not the vocabulary.**

Two questions could produce real findings. **Determinism**: a match record carries a seed, so flips must reproduce on replay, and a second source of randomness would desync a replay while passing every board-level test. And **"for each tails"** — one row counts the opposite face, so if no printed sentence separates the two readings, that's D448's confound again and the test has to construct the board the print never provides.

I also flagged that this may be the slice where D450's reachability argument for the version *doesn't* apply, since coin prompts can park.

text:
**D452 is committed** (`0927564e`) and sweeping on pid 3919528. Verified: green at 449 files / 9,975 tests, precheck clean at 1,882, all 12 rows KILLED.

**My framing was wrong and so was my split.** There is no fold: the heads count has been spent into a **longer program** since D130 — *heads* copies of the ops, appended at the flip site — and no op ever reads a coin. And the axis I told it to price separately, the unbounded until-tails flip, is **free**: that flip count shipped at D129 and the family already has an arm using it. What costs is the *consequent*, identically for a printed 2 and for until-tails. I separated the cheap axis and merged the expensive one.

**Two shipped refusals fell, and both had named their own trigger.** One said the hand op *"would be the first op to consume `rngState`"* — it was built two hundred decisions ago and now derives off the bare sentence at 8 legal printings. The other said a park is *"the one thing this expansion cannot express"* — but the resume path ends in a run over the rest, so an op in the rest parks again, driven on a two-copy program. The builder disproved the capability claim and still shipped **2 printings rather than 4**, because the real cost is a witness re-point across five files.

**The audit's most valuable finding was an absence.** D130's entire family had **zero mutant rows since 0.81.0** — unpinned for 322 decisions behind a 1,459-line suite. Two rows were written for it and one **survived the first probe**, exposing a rung whose comment claimed a leading anchor while its own leading word was lowercase: the sentence was refused by **case**, never by the anchor.

And a pinned "out of scope" sentence turned out to print **zero times** — it was one card's opening glued to another card's consequent, 97 characters, green since D130. The set was rebuilt with every entry asserted to be a real corpus row.

**D452's sweep landed exactly** — `1853 killed · 29 known`. Closed in `c2c280ce`. Thirteen for thirteen.

**The figure this sweep settles is the one the slice couldn't.** `programPerHeads` had **zero mutant rows for 322 decisions**, so every green sweep since 0.81.0 said nothing whatever about that family — a corpus reports only on the rows it *contains*, and a family with no rows is indistinguishable from a family that passes. The two rows added here are the first evidence it discriminates at all, and one **survived its first probe**: not merely unpinned, but a live hole.

That's now a convention, and it names a gap in the process itself. All four pre-probe passes ask what an edit might **break** — which rows mention what's changing, which sit in an edited span, which no longer occur once, which changed nothing. **None asks what was never covered.** So: when you touch a mechanism, grep the corpus for rows naming it *before* assuming the sweep's history covers it. An empty result is a finding, and it's the cheapest one available.

detail: 6 uncovered EffectOp kinds found; analyzing coverage pattern
text:
**D453 turns D452's newest convention on the whole op union — and the cheap version already found something.**

Of **69 declared `EffectOp` kinds**, **six have zero mutant rows naming them** — `boostAttack`, `clearStatus`, `moveCountersChosen`, `moveCountersToDefender`, `opponentMayDraw`, `preventChosenAttack` — and seventeen more have only one or two. This one buys **zero printings by design**, which is the right trade: the residue that remains is guarded by real mechanisms, while these are shipped ops that every green sweep has been silent about.

Three things I asked for beyond the rows. **Why six escaped** — that's a pattern, not six accidents, and the shared cause predicts where the next gap is, which is worth more than the rows themselves. **Whether "no row naming it" is even the right predicate** — mine is a substring match over row text, a floor rather than a census, since a row can pin an op by mutating a line inside its implementation without ever naming it; I asked for a better measurement and for both numbers. And **whether the thin seventeen are covered or merely non-zero**, spot-checked rather than assumed.

I also flagged that some of these ops may have **zero legal printings**, in which case a mutant is `unreachable-population` rather than a live guard — a different verdict that must be declared up front, not discovered by the sweep. And that this is likely the run's first genuinely **non-monotone** prediction since D444, which is the informative case.

detail: predicate failure analysis: 74 kinds, 11 unpinned found; mechanism identified
text:
**D453 is committed** (`52ff4307`) and sweeping on pid 4039430. Verified: check **identical** to D452 at 449 files / 9,975 tests — which is itself the measurement, since a coverage slice that moved a test count would have been building something. Precheck clean at 1,900; probe 17 killed + 1 declared.

**Both of my counts died on the first measurement, and the predicate failed in the direction that matters.** There are **74 distinct kinds over 76 members**, not 69 — two names are declared twice. And "no row names it" isn't a floor, it's **wrong in both directions**: good rows quote a *field* or a *line* rather than the op's name, so a 13-row op read as unpinned, while several "covered" ops had only prose mentions inside another row's description. The false-positive direction is the one that stops you looking. The replacement predicate — does a row's `find` **span** intersect any region that implements or produces the kind — found **11** unpinned against my 8, overlapping in the 6 I named.

**Why they escaped is a mechanism, and it predicts the next gap.** Tagging every op-region hit gives **758 producer-side against 358 implementation-side, with 24 kinds producer-only and zero implementation-only** — coverage is a strict chain, because a row gets written by the slice that *builds a sentence* and is about the arm it just wrote. The predictor is **field count**, not importance: mean declared keys beyond `op` is **1.00** for the unpinned, **1.60** for the thin, **3.00** for the covered. One unpinned op has 29 printings and a single field. A derivation-arm row is a row about a *field*, so a field-free op is invisible to the corpus however much behaviour its implementation carries.

**Two findings beyond the rows.** A survivor was read as a suite hole and turned out to be none of my three categories — it was an **over-narrow `expectKilledBy`** naming suites that never load the line, which the harness reports as a GAP. For a registry-only op, that field is a question about the **card**, not the kind. And a shipped doc block had claimed since D216 that a row was *"recorded as an equivalent mutant"* — in a file that didn't contain it. A claim about the corpus, written into the engine, unchecked for 237 decisions. It's true now.

**D453's sweep landed exactly** — `1870 killed · 30 known`. Closed in `5fcb68ce`. Fourteen for fourteen.

**This was the first non-monotone prediction since D444, and that's what makes it worth reading.** A monotone `+N, +0` follows from counting the rows you added and survives being sloppy. This one required knowing in advance that **exactly one of eighteen** new rows would be declared rather than killed — and which one.

The `+1` is the arity row whose equivalence a shipped doc block had asserted **since D216, in a file that did not contain it**. So the prediction and the finding are the same object: the slice could only name `+1` because it had established what that row was, and it could only establish that by discovering the claim had never been recorded. A coverage slice's delta is its thesis, not its receipt.

`bun run check` is **unchanged across the entire slice** — 449 files / 9,975 tests, before and after. For a coverage slice that's the measurement, not an absence of one.

**Run state:** engine **0.354.0** (deliberately not bumped), `MATCH_RECORD_VERSION` 29, corpus **1,900**, ratchet **123**, tree clean, fourteen slices closed (D440–D453), nothing pushed.

The most useful thing carried forward is the predictor D453 measured: **coverage follows field count, not importance**. Mean declared keys beyond `op` run 1.00 for unpinned kinds, 1.60 for thin ones, 3.00 for covered — because a row gets written by the slice that builds a *sentence*, and such a row is about a *field*. Field-poor ops are invisible to the corpus however much behaviour they carry. Ten thin ops remain, priced and named.

detail: D454 implementation coverage analysis; 3 key questions identified
text:
**D454 continues on the implementation side**, which D453 measured as systematically thin rather than merely uneven: **758 producer-side rows against 358 implementation-side, 24 kinds producer-only, and zero implementation-only.** Coverage is a strict chain, because rows get written by the slice that builds a sentence, and such a row is about the arm it just wrote.

I picked this over returning to the residue for one reason: **it targets a demonstrated defect class, not a hypothetical one.** The two worst defects of this whole stretch were both implementation-side and **neither was caught by a test** — an op that aimed *across the table* because a ternary let a new member fall out of the `else`, and another that silently dropped own-side refs, producing a real prompt, a real answer and zero damage. Both were caught by the compiler and the audit. Rows on those lines are the guard that was missing.

Three questions carry the analytical weight. Whether the **chain still holds** after D453 added 18 rows — including whether its own rows were producer- or implementation-side. Whether **field count is still the predictor**, or whether pinning the field-poor ops moved the means in a way that shows the correlation was an artefact of authoring order. And the one that matters most for anyone continuing this: **what "covered enough" means for an implementation** — per branch, per guard, per side effect — measured against its own proposal rather than asserted. A number you can re-run beats an adjective.

detail: D454 committed; verified slice falsified D453 findings; mechanism sound, inference inverted
text:
**D454 is committed** (`8f8e0c06`) and sweeping on pid 4150527. Verified: check unchanged at 449 files / 9,975 tests, precheck clean at 1,912, 12 killed with no survivors.

**The slice's main result is that D453's headline finding was an instrument artefact — and D453's own commit falsified it.** "Zero kinds implementation-only" came from an **asymmetric predicate**: wide producer regions, implementation regions stopping at the `case` arm. Widening the implementation side reproduces D453's totals to ~2% and returns **five** implementation-only kinds; following the call graph transitively returns **six**. Under both, zero is wrong. And D453's own eighteen rows are **seventeen implementation-side** — the slice that stated the chain broke it in the same commit.

That was findable because D453's audit script **was never committed**, so its numbers were unfalsifiable as published. Both replacement predicates here are stated with their construction so the next slice can re-run them.

**My brief inherited D453's recommendation and it didn't survive either.** Three of the five named targets are already pinned — they share a delegate carrying five rows — and a fourth was never thin. Only one was real. The honest target set turned out to be the **producer-only** kinds.

**And the mechanism was right while the inference was inverted.** Field count predicts the *producer* seat and points backwards for the implementation: 0.92 mean fields for implementation-only kinds against 1.92 for producer-only — with one op falsifying the rule outright at zero fields and 104 producer rows.

The semantic pass found the substantive gap: four identifiers, including **an entire status-immunity gate**, had zero rows in the whole corpus — executable by nothing. And the stopping rule I asked for came back **proposed and measured**: seat-line coverage moved 0.379 → 0.404, with one line deliberately left uncovered rather than widening a `find` to buy a digit.

detail: D453/D454 sweep pair closed (30 killed); audit corpus integrity review complete
text:
**D454's sweep landed exactly** — `1882 killed · 30 known`. Closed in `16ab203f`. Fifteen for fifteen.

**The D453/D454 pair is the clearest demonstration this run has produced that a green sweep cannot audit its own corpus.** Both sweeps were green, both predictions landed — and between them, one slice's headline structural claim turned out to be an **artefact of its own instrument**: reproducible to ~2% by a predicate built to match it, and false under the predicate built to be right. The sweep verified every row in both slices and had nothing to say about whether they were the *right* rows. A sweep answers *do these rows still discriminate*; only a re-derivation answers *is this the set that should exist*.

What made the error survivable is that **D453's audit script was never committed**, so its numbers couldn't be re-run until D454 rebuilt them. Hence the convention: **publish the instrument, not only the number.** A measurement whose script isn't in the tree is a claim. This run has now had one such claim survive four days and another survive 237 decisions.

**Run state:** engine **0.354.0** (unbumped through both coverage slices), `MATCH_RECORD_VERSION` 29, corpus **1,912**, ratchet **124**, tree clean, sixteen slices closed (D440–D454), nothing pushed. `bun run check` is unchanged at 449 files / 9,975 tests across both — the intended measurement for coverage work.

My *sub-family guesses* have been wrong nearly every slice — twice I named a "clean split" that wasn't the real blocker at all. So this brief **hands over the measured family and deliberately does not say where to cut**. The builder's first job is a **per-row blocker table**, established by running the readers and splitters and diffing each unread row against its nearest *built* neighbour — not by reading the sentence and inferring.

That instruction has direct evidence behind it: D447 found seven rows of one group refused for **five different reasons**. Assuming a shared blocker is how a slice ends up building a mechanism that buys nothing.

I did list candidate hypotheses — that the reveal-to-hand destination may already ship, that "in any combination" may already be a flat cap over a union, that owner-prefixed nouns have their filter — but explicitly framed them as things to **falsify cheaply**, not a plan. text:

**The per-row blocker table was the point, and it broke my framing.** "13 sentences don't resolve" is true of **readers** and false of **builds** — four of the thirteen, six printings, are already built through the registry. Worse: the census asserts `resolvedByAnyReader === false` for registry sentences, so writing a reader arm for any of those four would have **reddened the census** until its registry row was retired. Two files of churn for zero printings. A slice that cut where the sentences merely *looked* cheapest would have rebuilt four things that already work.

That's exactly why the brief withheld the cut. Every blocker was isolated by a **minimal pair** — the same sentence with one axis changed — rather than by reading it, and that's what found the real target: the batch rule was the only group blocked by **one** axis, and its anchor already matched. The arm was refusing on a *condition*, not on the text.

**D235's refusal fell after 222 decisions**, and for the now-familiar reason: *"unrepresentable here, representable one op over"* was true of the neighbouring op's count field and false of this one, because this park answers with a **map** — so the printed rule is a constraint on the map, which is a flag.

**And the version case is the one the last three coverage slices waved through.** The field rides a continuation and the persisted choose phase, so a park is the *road* to storage. Loss was shown to be a relaxation rather than corruption, **and detectable elsewhere in the record** — the caption is built from the same field, so a park captioned for one target without the rider is a byte string this deploy cannot write.

One measurement worth keeping: **opcoverage moved by zero**, before and after, on a slice that rewrote this op's arm, park, caption, validator and both HUDs. That's a fact about the predicate, not about the slice.

That's the instrument reporting its own predicate honestly. It counts lines that **resolve a seat**, and a batch-versus-spread constraint resolves no seat. A coverage number measures the axis it was built for and is silent on every other — which is exactly why D455 was required to publish its blind spots alongside it. The successor lesson: don't read a flat figure as *"this slice added no safety"*; read it as *"this slice moved no seat lines"*, and if the safety it added matters, the answer is a **second predicate**, not a bigger number on this one.

And the destination is shared (*"attach them to your Pokémon in any way you like"*), which the printed sentence reads as **one** distribution; if separate ops produce two, that's observable and needs a board.

detail: D458 committed; D457 anchor blocker analyzed; preconditions enforced
text:
**D458 is committed** (`2c1ae44b`) and sweeping on pid 432960. Verified: green at 449 files / **10,009 tests**, precheck clean at 1,966, all 10 rows KILLED on the first run.

**D457's estimate held on the ops and fields and failed on the anchor — the second mis-priced blocker in this family in two slices.** The note said *"a different sentence shape, so its own arm by D232's rule."* D232's rule, **opened and read**, says the opposite: a family collapses to **one** arm when its sentences differ in a *noun*, and splits on a *verb*. This row differs in the noun **count** alone. Both mis-pricings share a shape — written as facts about a *sentence*, they were claims about a *carrier*.

**The two preconditions that make two ops equal one sentence are now enforced rather than assumed.** A second noun is refused beside a single-target destination, because two maps would put one batch on one body and the other elsewhere; and beside the record-filing tail, where two ops sharing one slot means the second **overwrites** the first — so a board where one search attached and the other whiffed would answer *no* about an attach that happened. Both are zero-printing refusals read off the model.

The shared-destination question got the answer worth having: two distributions are observably equivalent to one **because and only because nothing couples the batches** — disjoint pools, every target still eligible, no map constraint. That's a reason, not a coincidence.

Two process notes. `precheck` reported BROKEN twice, once from a **one-line lint fix** that moved a mutant's anchor — caught in seconds where the sweep would have taken ninety minutes. And the bare arithmetic operand that **seven consecutive slices** stepped late is now *named* rather than carrying an eighth warning above it.

One priced a field against a *neighbouring* op's vocabulary; the other priced an arm against a rule that says the **opposite** when opened rather than cited. Both were phrased as facts about a **sentence** and were claims about a **carrier** — what the engine can express versus what one op, anchor or rule happens to hold today. One had stood 222 decisions.

The cheap disproof for both is a single line: **delete one axis from the printed string and re-ask the readers.** D458 ran it, found the remainder had derived since D235, and located the blocker exactly at zero cost. That's now a convention — re-read a refusal as naming a *carrier*, work out which carrier would actually serve the sentence, and re-measure the population against that one rather than the one that refused it.

detail: D459: validating cheap axis-deletion test (17/24 rows work)
text:
**D459 turns D458's disproof into a committed instrument.**

The reasoning: **targeting has been the weakest part of the last ten slices.** A handed-forward list was wrong three slices running, and the same family mis-priced its own blocker twice. Meanwhile D458 proved the cheap mechanical test — *delete one axis from the printed string and re-ask the readers* — locates a blocker exactly, at zero cost, where reading prose had failed twice.

I ran a crude version over the residue first: **17 sentences / 24 printings have a one-axis deletion whose remainder already derives.** So the approach yields something, and the slice is worth doing.

Three constraints matter. It must use the **canonical four-way residue**, because D457 found rows that read as unbuilt and are registry-built — a classifier reporting those as buildable would be worse than none. It must **cross-check against the record**, comparing its verdicts to the reasons D440–D458 wrote down, with disagreements resolved in the instrument's favour. And it must publish its blind spots, starting with the one my probe already exposes: **a deletion that derives can point at the wrong half** — for two rows the readable remainder is a rider, while the head is a mechanism nobody has built.

Then it uses its own output to pick and build the cheapest real target — or ships the classifier alone and says so, which is a legitimate outcome rather than a shortfall.

detail: D459 closed; sweep complete, 68% residue opaque, targeting failures identified
text:
**D459's sweep landed exactly** — `1943 killed · 31 known`. Closed in `95f4224b`. Twenty for twenty.

**The sweep was the least informative thing this slice produced, and that's the result.** It cost ~2.3 hours to answer a question the probe had already answered in 34 seconds. What it *couldn't* answer — *is the residue mostly cheap or mostly hard?* — took the committed classifier, and came back **`OPAQUE` 88 / 126: 68% of the residue by sentence.**

Read against the record's own errors, that's the case for mechanical targeting. Three slices cited corpus rows by **array index** against a convention written to forbid it. One family mis-priced its own blocker **twice**. A handed-forward list was wrong **three slices running**. Every one is a *targeting* failure, and none would have been caught by any sweep, however green.

Two requirements make such an instrument trustworthy, both learned here. **Print the value, not only the verdict** — ten rows were one-token deletions and nine lost the token's meaning in the derived value, a spelling blocker against nine semantic ones, which no count can separate. And **a class is a lower bound on the work, never an estimate** — the instrument's own blind spot fires on the record's rows, so it has to say *which half* of a compound survived.

**Run state:** engine **0.358.0**, `MATCH_RECORD_VERSION` 29, corpus **1,974**, ratchet **129**, tree clean, twenty-two slices closed (D440–D459), nothing pushed. `bun run check` at 449 files / **10,019 tests**. Canonical residue **129 sentences / 180 printings**.

Two instruments now live in the tree — `opcoverage.ts` for the op union, `residue-census.ts` for the printed residue — and between them they've corrected four published figures that no test could have caught.

detail: D460 classifier surfaces coin-flip threshold patterns; analyzing 4 follow-up questions
text:
**D460 is the first slice to be targeted *by* the classifier rather than by my reading of the corpus.**

I ran it, and it did the job immediately. `COMPOUND-head` is the largest non-opaque class, and inside it sits a cluster where the instrument shows the **head already deriving** to a coin reading and names the **tail as the entire blocker** — a threshold over the flip results applying a status:

*"…If **either of them is heads**, your opponent's Active Pokémon is now Paralyzed"* · *"…If **both of them are tails**"* · *"…If **at least 2 of them are heads**"*

Three predicates over one vector, one mechanism, and the status side already ships. That's the shape the classifier exists to surface — and notably, the output prints the *derived value* of the surviving half, which is how it distinguishes "the head builds" from "something builds".

Four questions carry it. Where the **faces** live, since D452 established the flip happens before the program and returns faces rather than a count. Whether the three thresholds are **one parameterised comparison or three cases** — with the wrinkle that *"both are tails"* over two coins is just *"zero heads"*, so the tails form may be redundant. Whether the **immunity gate** refuses correctly, since a status silently succeeding past it is the defect class D454 pinned. And **composition** — whether a sentence can carry both a coin reading and an effect, which D445 found was a habit rather than a property the last time it came up.
D460 has finished with the classifier and started writing — `effects.ts` first.

detail: D461 analysis: filter vs scope axis on board position narrowing
text:
**D461 takes the filtered heal**, again chosen by running the classifier rather than reading the corpus.

It surfaces a `PHRASE-1` cluster where the blocker is a **single printed word** — *"each of your **Basic** Pokémon"*, *"each of your **Benched** Pokémon"*, *"1 of your Benched **Ancient** Pokémon"*. Deleting that word yields a string that builds, so the verb, the amount and the destination all ship; what can't be expressed is **which bodies get healed**.

The important caveat is one D459 measured: these are **semantic** deletions, not spelling ones. Nine of ten one-token deletions lose the token's meaning in the derived value, and all three of these do — so the classifier is saying *where* the blocker is, not that it's a one-line change.

The sharpest question is whether **filter and scope are the same axis**. *"Basic"* narrows by a card property; *"Benched"* narrows by a **board position** — and `matchesFilter` never sees an in-play body, a boundary re-confirmed as recently as D450, where the resolution was that the *op* can carry a board rider even though the filter cannot. So this is either one parameter or two, and the union's own discriminator rule decides it.

I also asked for the survivor analysis to name individually anything that could plausibly move — D460's entire `+0` value sat in two rows that couldn't be dismissed by file.

text:
**D462 is committed** (`d61f972d`) and sweeping on pid 941958. Verified: green at **452 files / 10,108 tests**, precheck clean at 2,011, all 4 rows KILLED.

**Withholding the target worked.** The classifier's *printed derived value* is what selected it — deleting three tokens yields a single status op, so the blocked half is just two more of something shipped long ago. Zero mechanism. And the builder enumerated everything it rejected with a measured price, including one row it refused **twice**: building it would have silently un-armed two attribution controls that depend on it staying unread.

**D424 measured this row, named it, and left it unbuilt on a reason that prices the wrong thing.** Its population claim was true and re-measured — 33 candidate rows, exactly one Oxford list — but the inference doesn't follow: the rule it invoked prices a **new parameter**, and this anchor adds none. That's the seventh refusal to fall in thirteen slices, and the fourth whose *measurement* was right while its *conclusion* wasn't.

The template-over-literal choice is subtle and correct: same cost either way, but a literal's three words are provably slot-disjoint, which would make the collision refusal **unreachable** from the new arm.

**Four things went wrong and were caught.** Six frozen endpoints were stepped before the front-term rule was re-read — a red run *reports the endpoint*, so the wrong edit is the one the tool names. And a `String.replace` with an unescaped `$` in the pattern **spliced 19,000 lines of a source file into itself**, caught by a line count and restored from the HEAD blob.

On the suffix column, my brief was wrong in the builder's favour: **the ingest code isn't missing** — a migration was never applied, so production has no column at all, and the facet endpoint selects it inside a shared batch. The Ancient/Future banner also re-measured at **12 sentences / 16 printings**, needing its predicate in at least four carriers.

text:
**D462's sweep landed exactly** — `1980 killed · 31 known`. Closed in `ea778696`. Twenty-three for twenty-three.

**It's the smallest delta of the run — four rows — on a slice whose most expensive moment no instrument here can see.** A `String.replace` whose pattern ended `\.$` before a backtick **spliced 19,000 lines of `effects.ts` into itself**, because `$` is special in a *replacement* string and `` $` `` inserts everything preceding the match. The sweep can't see that. `precheck` can't — the `find` still occurs once. None of the four pre-probe passes can. It was caught by a **line count**, 25,970 → 45,031, and undone from the HEAD blob.

That's now a convention alongside D459's `try/finally`: a patch script must use a **function** replacement, which never interprets, **and assert its own file's size after writing**. Every instrument in this repo reads those files assuming they're source — a corrupted one isn't a failed edit, it's a false baseline for everything that runs next.

The slice's own finding was the seventh refusal to fall in thirteen slices, and again the measurement was right while the conclusion wasn't: *"the only 3-status row in the column, so a template would be a literal over a pool of one"* — true about the **sentence**, but the rule it invoked prices a **parameter**, and this anchor adds none.

detail: D463 running, classifier target selection; residue 71% opaque
text:
**D463 is running, again choosing its own target from the classifier.**

**The target wasn't in the class table, and finding out why is the slice's first result.** The classifier's span probe splits and rejoins on spaces, so a deletion reaching the last token takes the sentence-final period with it and the remainder can never build. A tail-aware variant reaches **18 sentences / 24 printings** of the residue, six of them sitting in `OPAQUE`. The instrument's blind spot was found **by using it**, not by reading it — and deliberately *not* fixed in the same slice, since changing the instrument that picked your target leaves nothing to check the pick against.

**D462's doc block named the wrong byte.** It said the row was *"refused by the second capture group and by nothing else"*. Measured across all 640 rows, that anchor claims exactly one row under **every** single-axis loosening, and this row is in none — it demands a comma the row never prints. The byte actually doing the work was a different anchor's terminator, so the re-point went onto the set the probe *names* rather than the set the prose claimed.

And a nice observation: **the same loud-control slot has been re-pointed twice in three slices, each time onto the row the next slice built** — a loud-control list is a targeting instrument in disguise.

Three findings came from driving rather than reasoning. The discard op **collapses interchangeable candidates before deciding to park**, so a board of three identical Energy never reaches a continuation and a driver written against it would have tested nothing. The two ends of an anchor **fail differently**, because a trailing near-miss isn't loud when the splitter can compose the newly-claimable head with a claimed tail. **D470 is committed (`34823c80`) and its sweep is running** (pid 1975174, 2,113 rows). This one found a real defect in the tooling.

**The mutation harness itself carried the `$`-splice bug** — the exact class this repo's conventions have banned in hand-written probes since D462. `run.ts` applied every mutant with `text.replace(find, replace)`, a *string* second argument, so `` $` `` in a replacement splices the entire preceding file. Every anchor row quotes its own regex in a doc comment, and a pattern ending `…$` before a backtick spells that directive exactly. **11 of 2,113 rows corrupted, ten of them since D234** — I confirmed the count independently rather than taking it on report.

Why it lasted 236 slices: **the corruption read as success.** A spliced file doesn't parse, vitest exits non-zero, the row reports KILLED. It surfaced only because the mirror image is loud — the same corruption on a *declared survivor* throws a spurious `STALE-SURVIVOR` and fails the run. The declared survivors turn out to be the only rows whose corruption is observable at all.

Fixed in one line, guarded by a new `splice-gate.ts` imported by `precheck` but deliberately *outside* it, so the guard's own mutant isn't over-determined. All ten pre-existing rows re-measured under the literal replacement: **all ten genuinely KILLED** — I re-verified each individually, which is how I found that `--only` doesn't accumulate (ten flags in one invocation silently runs one row and prints a green-looking total). So no coverage gap was hidden; the fix changes no verdict, it changes what the verdicts mean.

The slice's own row also landed: file line 558, the `Iono's` subgroup noun on a board-wide Energy count. The caller enumeration I asked for first corrected the price I'd inherited — **three consumers, not two ops**, the third being a `BoardCondition` no brief had ever named.

Gates verified: check GREEN 459/10,328, precheck 2,113 (now reporting the literal-patch property), gate §A 138/112/156, probe 15 killed · 2 survivors · 0 GAP. Predicted line: **`2076 killed · 37 known survivor(s)` over 2,113** — with the caveat, recorded before the run, that if one of the ten formerly-spliced rows comes back a survivor, that's the old defect having hidden a genuine gap, not a regression.

detail: analyzed classifier markers & controls; 5/6 refuted, attribution inverted
text:
Tree untouched — the agent is in its evidence-gathering phase, which is what a brief that asks for a justified choice should produce.

It chose (B) — the `OPAQUE` anatomy, with a gate alongside the instrument, which is D465's rule honoured. Checking whether the flagged diagnostics are real or just how this repo's scripts are typed.

The diagnostics are noise — `residue-census.ts` uses both `import.meta.main` and `process.` and passes, because `scripts/` isn't in any tsconfig project (`tsconfig.json` has `"files": []`). Same shape as the shipped instruments. Letting it run.

Still iterating on the two instrument files — the classifier partition is the hard part of this slice.

Mutant rows now being authored against its own classifier — the D465 requirement that an instrument be killable by the corpus.

All gates confirmed and `packages/` is byte-unchanged, so the agent was right to refuse the version bump. Verifying its correction of the stale conventions figure with the instrument itself.

Confirmed: attack-copy is **6 / 13**, not the 7 / 14 the conventions have claimed. Running the ritual, including that correction.

**D471 is committed (`7c5ff2da`) and its sweep is running** (pid 2096562, 2,120 rows). This one was a measurement slice, and it overturned an assumption that had been steering targeting for four slices.

**`OPAQUE` isn't "the hard ones" — it's mostly "the ones with two separated edits."** All three probes in the census are single-region: one segment, one span, one contiguous substitution. A sentence differing from a built one at two *separated* points is invisible to every one of them, however small each difference is. Measured: **33 REACHED / 45 FAR**, and eleven of the reached are two small edits from a built string. The class had been read as a difficulty ranking when it was really a statement about the probe's vocabulary.

Two things I'd flag as the substance beyond the headline:

**Five of six proposed markers were refuted by their own control.** The most plausible story about `OPAQUE` — that it's the continuing-effect seam — is false by **49 built sentences / 217 printings** carrying that same marker. A marker that appears on built sentences explains nothing; that's now a convention requiring a built-side control before any blocker may label a row.

**The attribution control came back inverted, and that's the finding.** With the classifier's central function mutated to its nearest wrong sibling, its own gate went red while `bun run check` at 459 files / 10,328 tests exited 0 — along with every other instrument, the linter, and precheck. Nothing in this repo can see a defect in a committed measurement except the gate you write for it. That's D465's rule as a measurement rather than a warning.

The agent also **refused three of my instructions and was right on all three**: my decisive argument against the alternative slice (the "basic"/Luminous semantics) was false — it's settled and shipped twice — so it declined that row on *price* instead, re-measured at 13 consumers across 21 call sites for one printing. And it refused the version bump and census pins because `packages/engine` is byte-unchanged and no sentence was built. `check` is identical on both sides, correctly.

It also found a stale figure the conventions have carried since they were written: the attack-copy rule said 7 sentences / 14 printings; it's **6 / 13**. Corrected in place. Predicted line: **`2083 killed · 37 known survivor(s)` over 2,120**.

detail: mutation testing analysis: 2094 killed, 37 survivors over 2131 decisions
text:
Tree untouched — the agent is investigating the eleven candidates. (The two flagged files are its scratch scripts in the job tmp dir, outside the repo.)

Building — `effects.ts` plus census tax, and `defenderStatusTriple.test.ts` in the mix suggests it took the `{N}` Paralyzed row. The `interpreter.ts` diagnostic is mid-edit; `bun run check` is the arbiter and the agent runs it.

16 files, no new suite file yet — still mid-build.

Confirmed — new suite `typedActiveStatusGate.test.ts`. It took candidate 3, the `{N}` type-gated status row, which is the joint-highest printing count among those that pass the schema test. 62 paths now (version + census tax).

Stale — `resolveKoPrizes` no longer appears in that file; the agent had it mid-edit. Continuing to wait.

Mutant rows authored (+117), and the scratch file named `inert.ts` says it's running the find-vs-replace diff. Gates in progress.

Steady at 62 — the agent is in its gate runs (`check` alone takes ~2.5 min and has needed several rounds each slice).

The agent caught two errors in my brief, including a wrong citation — my "D468 built this axis for `{L}`" was actually D367. Verifying the gates independently.

Confirmed — line 537 *is* the fourth home, so building it owes a fifth. My brief was off by one. Running the ritual.

**D472 is committed (`5ae6788c`) and its sweep is running** (pid 2237696, 2,131 rows). The shortlist D471 built paid out on its first use — this row cost **one anchor and one arm**, in a class that had been static for four slices and read as "the hard ones."

The interesting part isn't what was built but what was *refused*. The obvious anchor captures the subject: `^If (.+), it is now (STATUS)\.$`. Measured over all 640 corpus rows, that wider form claims **exactly the same 1 sentence / 2 printings** — it buys nothing. And it costs a wrong program, because the consequent is an anaphor: under the wide form, *"If you have any {M} Pokémon on your Bench, it is now Paralyzed."* resolves and paralyses the **defender** off a pronoun pointing at the attacker's own Bench. **An anchor that generalises the subject silently generalises the referent**, and no census can see it — the sentence still reads, the residue still falls.

Two other things worth keeping:

**A boolean consequent has no number**, so the usual "N wrong builds answer N different numbers" board doesn't apply. The answer was a five-board signature read as five bits — correct build 17, eight wrong builds at eight distinct values, all seven measured against the real predicate rather than asserted in a comment.

A slice that adds a third member to an unpinned union and pins only its own arm has made the union harder to change, not easier.

text:
1926/2,163 — final stretch.

The sweep produced no summary line and left the tree dirty — that's an anomaly. Investigating.

False alarm — the runner is alive (pid 2514215) and the dirty file was simply the mutant applied mid-row; it's already restored. My `alive()` check raced. Resuming the poll.

Exactly as predicted, and the tree is clean. Verifying completeness structurally.

**D474 is closed out and committed** (`4f646100`). Starting D475 — the row D474 both priced and armed a trap for.

**D474 is fully closed** — sweep exact at `2125 killed · 38 known survivor(s) · 0 GAP(s)` over 2,163, completeness structural, 36th consecutive clean run. Close-out committed as `4f646100`. All ten debt rows came back killed under the real harness, confirming what the probe showed.

One correction to something I said mid-poll: I reported the sweep as anomalous — no summary line, dirty tree. **That was my monitoring being wrong, not the sweep.** At 2,148/2,163 the runner was simply holding a mutant applied mid-row before its `finally` restored the file, and my liveness check raced with `ps` and called a healthy run dead. The sweep finished normally.

Worth recording as a convention, which I did: **the only reliable done-signal is the summary line in the log** — never the working tree, never the process table. A sweep is a program that deliberately dirties the tree thousands of times; reading that dirtiness as damage inverts the meaning of the thing being watched. It's the same fact that makes `--allow-dirty` necessary and a clean start mandatory — the runner owns tree-dirtiness for the duration, so anyone else's is indistinguishable from its own.

**D475 is running**, on the row D474 both re-priced *downward* and armed a trap for. The interesting part is that this is the first row that can test whether D474's ternary→`switch` conversion actually bought anything: this member counts Energy, so its payload looks like `attachedEnergy`'s, and under the old dispatch it would have fallen **silently** into the self-attached reading. I've asked for that measured explicitly — whether the `switch` makes the wrong-member mutation loud. Either answer is a finding.
